name: Henrik Stenson
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Benson & Hedges International Open on the European Tour in 2001 at age 25, his first European Tour victory, after topping the Challenge Tour money rankings in 2000.
early_history_summary: Started golf at age 12 at Gullbringa Golf & Country Club near Gothenburg with local pro Richard Bayliss. Moved to southern Sweden in 1991, joined Barsebäck Golf & Country Club, reached scratch handicap at 18, and represented Sweden as a junior amateur. Turned professional in 1998 and topped the Challenge Tour Order of Merit in 2000 to earn his European Tour card.
family_context_summary: Born in Gothenburg, Sweden; moved with parents to Bjärred outside Malmö at age 15. Family occupation and class not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: golf club access, early coaching, Swedish golf system, junior competition
evidence_summary: Stenson started golf at 12 and received coaching from local pro Richard Bayliss at Gullbringa Golf & Country Club. He joined Barsebäck Golf & Country Club after moving to southern Sweden at 15, reaching scratch by 18. He represented Sweden as a junior amateur before turning pro in 1998 and topping the Challenge Tour in 2000. His first European Tour win came at 25 in 2001. Family financial background is not documented.
starting_point: Born in Gothenburg, Sweden to a family that moved to Bjärred near Malmö when he was 15; family occupation and class not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Resides in Orlando, Florida; plays on the European Senior Tour and European Tour; former world No. 2 golfer with 22 professional wins including the 2016 Open Championship.

trajectory.event: Represented Sweden at the European Boys' Team Championship as an amateur.
Turned professional and began playing on the Challenge Tour.
Topped the Challenge Tour money rankings to earn his European Tour card.
Won the Benson & Hedges International Open for his first European Tour victory.
Became the first Swede to win a World Golf Championships event at the Accenture Match Play.
Won the PGA Tour's flagship event, The Players Championship.
Won the FedEx Cup and Race to Dubai, finishing first in both the PGA Tour and European Tour season-long rankings.
Won the Open Championship, his first and only major, by three strokes over Phil Mickelson.

name: Viswanathan Anand
milestone_by_age_26: Became India's first chess grandmaster in 1988 at age 18, after winning the World Junior Chess Championship in 1987 and the Asian Junior Championship in 1984 and 1985; also became India's national chess champion at age 16.
early_history_summary: Learned chess at age six from his mother, a chess enthusiast. Won the sub-junior championship at 14 in 1983 with a perfect 9/9 score. Became the youngest Indian International Master at 15 in 1985. Won the World Junior Chess Championship in 1987 and earned the grandmaster title in 1988, both firsts for India. Awarded the Padma Shri at 18. Further developed skills while living in Manila in the late 1970s and early 1980s.
family_context_summary: Born in Mayiladuthurai, Tamil Nadu, India; father was a general manager at Southern Railways, mother was a housewife and chess enthusiast who taught Anand the game at age six. Family lived in Manila from 1978 to early 1980s while father worked as a consultant for the Philippine National Railways.
parent_family_domain_summary: Mother was a chess enthusiast who introduced Anand to the game at age six; father was a railway executive with no known chess background.
primary_early_advantage_tags: mother taught chess, early competitive immersion, cognitive prodigy, limited chess infrastructure in India
evidence_summary: Anand learned chess from his mother at age six and showed extraordinary early talent, winning the national sub-junior championship at 14 with a perfect score. He became India's first International Master at 15 and first grandmaster at 18, also winning the World Junior Championship in 1987. His father's railway job took the family to Manila, where he further developed his skills. Growing up in India with limited chess infrastructure was a constraint he overcame through self-driven practice and natural talent.
starting_point: Born in Mayiladuthurai, Tamil Nadu, India to a middle-class family; father was a general manager at Southern Railways and mother was a housewife and chess enthusiast.
current_position: Deputy President of FIDE since 2022; five-time World Chess Champion; FIDE rating 2739 as of 2025; resides in India.

trajectory.event: Became the youngest Indian to achieve the International Master title by winning the Asian Junior Championship for the second consecutive year.
Won the World Junior Chess Championship, the first Indian to do so.
Became India's first chess grandmaster and was awarded the Padma Shri, India's fourth-highest civilian award.
Qualified for his first Candidates Tournament in the World Chess Championship cycle.
Won the FIDE World Chess Championship by defeating Alexei Shirov.
Became the undisputed World Chess Champion by winning the tournament in Mexico City.
Defended the world title against Vladimir Kramnik in Bonn.
Elected Deputy President of FIDE, the international chess federation.

name: John Draper
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; was introduced to phone phreaking in 1969 at age 26 and gained fame as Captain Crunch via a 1971 Esquire profile at age 28.
early_history_summary: Son of a U.S. Air Force engineer; built a home radio station from discarded military components as a child. Enlisted in the Air Force in 1964, created a pirate radio station in Maine in 1967, and was discharged in 1968. Worked as an engineering technician at National Semiconductor and attended De Anza College before being introduced to phone phreaking in 1969.
family_context_summary: Son of a United States Air Force engineer; frequently bullied in school and briefly received psychological treatment.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a U.S. Air Force engineer; no evidence of domain-specific knowledge transfer relevant to computing or phreaking.
evidence_summary: John Draper was introduced to phone phreaking in 1969 at age 26, and his fame as Captain Crunch came with the 1971 Esquire profile at age 28. Before that, he served in the Air Force and worked as an electronics technician. No material milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Olafur Eliasson
milestone_by_age_26: Had a small solo show at age 15 at an alternative gallery in Denmark, but was still a student at the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts through 1995; major career milestones such as the Venice Biennale (2003) and The Weather Project at Tate Modern (2003) came after age 26.
early_history_summary: Born in Copenhagen to Icelandic immigrant parents; father was a cook who became an artist, mother a seamstress. Parents separated when he was 8. Had first solo show at 15 exhibiting landscape drawings at a small alternative gallery. Studied at the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts from 1989 to 1995, with a year in Cologne in 1993. Established Studio Olafur Eliasson in Berlin in 1995 at age 28.
family_context_summary: Born in Copenhagen to Icelandic immigrant parents; father was a cook who later became an artist, mother was a seamstress. Parents separated when he was 8; lived with mother and stepfather, a stockbroker. Spent summers with artist father in Iceland.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father became an artist and moved back to Iceland; exposure to father's artistic practice during summer visits may have influenced early interest in art.
evidence_summary: Olafur Eliasson had a small solo show at 15 but was still an art student through 1995, graduating at 28. His major career milestones came well after age 26. No material career-defining milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Bence Szabó

early_history_summary: Joined Újpesti TE fencing club in Budapest in 1974 at age 12 and trained under coaches Jakab László and Csaba Zarándi. Developed through the Hungarian fencing system, one of the world's strongest in sabre, reaching the senior national team level by the mid-1980s and winning Olympic team gold in 1988.
family_context_summary: Born in Budapest, Hungary; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Hungarian fencing tradition, Újpesti TE, dedicated coaches, team competition
evidence_summary: Szabó joined the Újpesti TE fencing club in Budapest at age 12 in 1974, training under coaches Jakab László and Csaba Zarándi. Hungary has a deep tradition in sabre fencing, providing an elite performance pipeline. He developed through the club and national team system to win Olympic team gold at 26 in 1988. Family background is not documented in reviewed sources.
starting_point: Born in Budapest, Hungary; family background and class not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Retired from competitive fencing; inducted into the FIE Hall of Fame in 2016; honorary citizen of Újpest.

name: Steve Irwin

name: Vladimir Tkachenko
milestone_by_age_26: Won Olympic bronze medal at the 1976 Montreal Games at age 19, followed by FIBA World Championship silver in 1978, EuroBasket gold in 1979, and the Euroscar and Mr. Europa awards as Europe's best player in 1979.
early_history_summary: Began playing professionally for Stroitel in the USSR Premiere League at age 16 in the 1973-74 season. His exceptional size (7'3" / 220 cm) and skill earned him a spot on the senior Soviet national team by 1976, where he won Olympic bronze at 19. He was named Europe's best player (Euroscar and Mr. Europa) at 22 in 1979 and won the FIBA World Championship gold in 1982 at 25.

The Soviet sports system provided elite training and competition access from a young age. Family background is not documented.
